A1.justification: Both PDFs are readable 11-page versions of SemTalk, with matching core methods and identifiable corresponding experiments, equations, and figures. Both end with references and contain no appendices; the supplementary material mentioned in their text is not included in either supplied PDF.

before.justification: V1 reports original BEAT2 and SHOW experiments, component ablations, generated-motion examples, and a user study involving 25 participants and 10 video samples.

after.justification: V3 retains these original empirical results and adds semantic-gate ablations, LivelySpeaker comparisons, and examples using different emotional deliveries of identical text.

M1.justification: The RVQ-VAE framework, hierarchical cross-attention, local/global rhythmic losses, semantic gating, alpha-blending, and threshold-based fusion remain. V3 names feature and loss weighting Wf/Wl and clarifies their operation, but the corresponding operations already appear in v1 Section 3.4 and Figure 3. The PDFs do not establish a changed procedure.

E1.justification: BEAT2-standard and SHOW remain the training and benchmark datasets. V3 Figure 9 adds a limited internet-speech test scenario using identical words with different emotional deliveries, expanding the input conditions explicitly examined.

E2.justification: V3 adds LivelySpeaker to the BEAT2 and SHOW quantitative and qualitative comparisons while retaining the existing comparators, including Habibie. Its Table 2 also introduces LivelySpeaker's SAG as a replacement comparator for the sparse-motion stage. The benchmark rows incorrectly cite Habibie reference [17], although LivelySpeaker is identified elsewhere as [52].

E3.justification: V3 Table 2 introduces semantic classification accuracy and controlled configurations involving random scores, separate weighting strategies, and SAG replacement with ground-truth semantic labels. The shared dataset splits, training budgets, thresholds, benchmark metrics, and 25-participant/10-video user-study design remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained component ablations in v1 Table 1/v3 Table 3, v3 Table 2 separately tests gate removal, random scores, feature weighting, loss weighting, and SAG substitution. Figure 9 additionally examines emotional sensitivity while holding text fixed. These additions substantially expand scrutiny of the central semantic-emphasis mechanism.

E5.justification: Both versions report point-valued experimental scores and average user-study ranks without run counts, random-seed specifications, uncertainty intervals, or significance tests. V3's random-score variant is an ablation control rather than a change in uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: The original benchmark values, component-ablation scores, and all user-study ranks are unchanged. V3 adds targeted results, including LivelySpeaker FGD values of 11.80 on BEAT2 and 32.17 on SHOW, semantic-gate accuracy of 82.76% versus 50.07% for random scores, and emotion-dependent motion examples. These are additional findings rather than improved scores for the retained SemTalk experiments.

T1.justification: V3 Section 3.1 removes the explicit motion-sequence and latent-space definitions and the quantization sequence given in v1's RVQ-VAE preliminaries. The five displayed equations retain their mathematical content apart from notation changes; no theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: Both versions claim that separately learning rhythmic base motion and sparse semantic motion, then adaptively combining them, improves holistic co-speech generation on two datasets. V3 highlights hierarchical cross-attention more prominently in the abstract and contributions, but v1 already describes that component and its intended role.

C2.justification: V3 adds explanations for face-to-hand-to-body guidance and attributes transition smoothness to the convolutional decoder. It interprets the new emotional examples and SAG comparison as evidence against text overfitting. It also changes the user-study emphasis from semantic consistency/diversity to semantic consistency/realism, consistent with the unchanged ranks.

D1.justification: V3 explains weighting and new ablation configurations more explicitly, but removes implementation details including ResNet blocks, code dimensionality, and fixing the masking ratio after epoch 120. It also drops the explanation that unsuccessful retraining caused ProbTalk's exclusion. Hardware, principal hyperparameters, and the project-page address remain.

R1.justification: V3 adds SynTalker and expands the discussion of already-cited LivelySpeaker through Section 3.4 and Figure 4, distinguishing conditioning inputs, frame-level versus global control, and latent-space integration. It also credits DiffSHEG in explaining hierarchical guidance. The overall positioning around separately modeling rhythm and sparse semantics remains.

P1.justification: Substantial rewriting and condensation affect the introduction, related work, RVQ-VAE preliminaries, method explanations, experimental setup, and qualitative discussion. V3 gives cross-attention its own paragraph heading, introduces explicit weighting terminology, and adds a dedicated comparison discussion while preserving the broad section sequence.

P2.justification: V3 substantially redraws the architecture diagram, adds the conceptual comparison in Figure 4, emotional examples in Figure 9, and semantic-gate Table 2. Existing qualitative displays gain LivelySpeaker panels and are resized or relocated. The original benchmark and component tables become Tables 1 and 3, with considerable rearrangement of the experimental pages.

improvement.justification: The new gate ablations and direct LivelySpeaker comparisons strengthen evidence for SemTalk's central semantic mechanism and clarify its relationship to similar work. These gains outweigh limited losses in implementation detail and the new benchmark citation error. The improvement remains modest: headline results are unchanged, and the claim that emotional responsiveness prevents text overfitting exceeds what the small qualitative example establishes.
